design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of the 1992 National Longitudinal Alcohol Epidemiologic Survey (NLAES), a US national multistage probability sample of 42,862 adults aged 18 and older in the noninstitutionalized population of the contiguous US and the District of Columbia, interviewed face to face by Census Bureau interviewers with the AUDADIS, a structured interview designed for lay interviewers. Among the 27,616 current and former drinkers, the weighted prevalence of lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence, and of lifetime alcohol abuse without dependence, was tabulated for each year of recalled age at first drink (12 or younger to 25 or older), overall and by sex and race; logistic regression estimated the change in odds per year of later onset, adjusted for sex, race, age group, duration of drinking, family history of alcoholism and current vs former drinking.
can_establish: That in a 1992 US household sample of people who had ever drunk alcohol, those who recalled starting to drink younger were much more likely to have met DSM-IV criteria for alcohol dependence or abuse at some time in their lives, and that the association remained after adjustment for sex, race, age group, family history, duration of drinking and current drinking status.
cannot_establish: Whether starting to drink early causes alcohol use disorders or whether the same family, genetic, behavioural and psychiatric factors lead to both (none was measured except a family-history question, and two adjustment variables may themselves follow from the disorder); whether the gradient holds for people outside households (who died, were institutionalized or were homeless); or how accurately adults recalled their age at first drink.

sample.recruitment: General-population household sample: the NLAES, sponsored by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, fieldwork by the US Bureau of the Census in 1992; multistage design with primary sampling units selected with probability proportional to size and oversampling of Black and young adult (18–29) respondents; about 92% of selected households and 97.4% of selected respondents took part (p. 104, Method › Study Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Current drinkers (drank in the past year) and former drinkers (drank in the past but not in the past year); lifetime abstainers, who have no onset age, are not analysed (p. 106). No minimum amount of drinking is stated in this paper.
sample.demographics: Among drinkers, 51% men and 49% women, 88.9% nonblack and 11.1% Black (p. 106, Results, 1st paragraph); these shares equal the unweighted counts (13,990 and 13,626; 24,554 and 3,062). Age, education and income distributions are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one interview). The numbers of drinkers missing an onset age or a diagnosis, and the number at each onset age, are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Household survivors only: people who had died (including from alcohol-related causes), were institutionalized or were homeless were not sampled, and early-onset, severe drinking may be over-represented among them. Respondents were aged 18 to over 65, so lifetime diagnoses cover very different lengths of drinking; age group and duration of drinking were adjusted for.

exposure.measurement: Age at onset of drinking: one recalled question asking how old the respondent was when they first started drinking, not counting small tastes or sips; test-retest reliability 0.72 (p. 105, Method › Measures, 3rd paragraph). Asked of adults of all ages in the same interview as the diagnostic questions; nothing recorded at the time.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Quantity and frequency of drinking were not analysed. Duration of drinking (years from onset to the last drink for former drinkers, or to the interview for current drinkers; set at 0.5 when onset and last drink were at the same age) was a covariate (p. 105).
exposure.polysubstance: Other drug use was neither measured in this analysis nor adjusted for.

comparison.controls: Drinkers with later recalled onset: prevalence tabulated for each year from 12 or younger to 25 or older (Tables 1 and 2, p. 107); regression per year of later onset, with onset entered as a continuous term (p. 108).
comparison.matching: None. Adjusted for sex, race (Black vs nonblack), age (18–24, 25–44, 45–64, 65+), duration of drinking, family history of alcoholism (any first- or second-degree relative reported as an alcoholic or problem drinker, asked about 18 types of relative) and current vs former drinking (pp. 105–106).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Childhood conduct problems, other psychopathology, childhood adversity, peer and family environment, genetic liability beyond the family-history question, and other drug use were not measured. Current vs former drinking, and duration of drinking up to the last drink in former drinkers, may themselves follow from having had the disorder.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS DSM-IV alcohol abuse and dependence, measured for the past year and before the past year with the DSM-IV clustering and duration criteria; lifetime = an episode in either period; the two diagnoses are mutually exclusive (lifetime abuse = abuse without lifetime dependence); test-retest reliability 0.76 (past year) and 0.73 (before the past year) (p. 105, Method › Measures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliabilities come from an independent general-population test-retest study (Grant et al., 1995) (p. 105); the recalled onset age has only a test-retest reliability (0.72), no validation.
outcomes.operationalization: Lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence; lifetime DSM-IV alcohol abuse among people without lifetime dependence.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (two outcomes, each also estimated in four subgroups).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (structured lay interview; onset and diagnostic questions asked in the same interview).

analysis.effect_sizes: Weighted prevalence by onset age (Tables 1 and 2, p. 107; see key findings). Adjusted: odds of lifetime dependence 14% lower and of lifetime abuse 8% lower per year of later onset; by subgroup, dependence 14.7% (men), 13.2% (women), 14.5% (nonblack), 8.1% (Black); abuse 7.0% (men), 9.1% (women), 6.7% (Black), 7.8% (nonblack) (p. 108). No odds ratios, confidence intervals, p values or unadjusted estimates are given. Editors' conversion: per-year odds ratios of about 0.86 (dependence) and 0.92 (abuse).
analysis.covariates: Sex, race, age group, duration of drinking, family history of alcoholism, current vs former drinking (p. 106, Statistical Analysis).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only percentage reductions in odds are reported: no regression table, no confidence intervals, no estimate before adjustment, no test of the sex or race differences in slope, and no number of drinkers at each onset age.
analysis.power: Not reported; 27,616 drinkers overall; cell sizes per onset age unknown (standard errors reach 9.9 points for Black respondents starting at 13).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Lifetime alcohol dependence was reported by 40.6% to 47.3% of drinkers who recalled starting at 14 or younger, 24.5% at 17, 16.6% at 18, about 10% at 21 to 22 and 7.9% at 25 or older, with a rise to 14.7% and 13.6% at 23 and 24; lifetime abuse without dependence peaked at 13.8% for onset at 14 and fell to 2.5%. After adjustment, the odds of dependence were 14% and of abuse 8% lower for each later year of onset.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion opens by calling age at first use "a powerful predictor of lifetime alcohol abuse and dependence" (p. 108); the Results call it a major contributor to the development of abuse and alcoholism (p. 108); the Discussion identifies ages 16 and younger as a particularly vulnerable period for starting to drink and suggests prevention aimed at delaying onset until after 18 or 19, while saying this should be considered cautiously (pp. 108–109). The authors also state that a prospective study is needed to learn whether the delay itself or, more likely, other associated factors explain the association, whether early onset is a modifiable risk factor or a marker, and to reduce the recall bias of cross-sectional designs including this one (p. 109). Gaps: (1) 'contributor to the development' and 'vulnerable period' are causal readings of a cross-sectional association with recalled onset, which the authors' own closing paragraph concedes; (2) the per-year figures come without confidence intervals or unadjusted estimates, and one linear term summarizes a curve that is steep before 18 and irregular after 20; (3) the thresholds of 16 and of 18 or 19 are read from the crude curve, not tested; (4) adjustment for current drinking status and, in former drinkers, for duration up to the last drink may remove part of the association or add bias, since both can follow from the disorder.

timeline.event: This study: cross-sectional NLAES association between recalled age at first drink and lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence and abuse.
Same survey and authors, for drugs among people who had used a drug at least 12 times: adjusted odds about 5% (abuse) and 4% (dependence) lower per year of later onset (read in this round).

Systematic review of prospective cohorts of age at first drink and adult alcohol problems: four cohorts, associations in some analyses and not others, often shrinking with adjustment; it cites this study among the mostly cross-sectional evidence behind guidance (as recorded on the library's card sc_maimaris_2014).

Minnesota twins: drinking by 14 stayed associated with adult alcohol outcomes after propensity weighting and within discordant pairs, but within identical pairs the association with alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms was not significant (as recorded on the library's claim on early drinking, which cites the study).

replication.where_it_stands: This cross-sectional association is the usual starting point for the question; whether early drinking causes later disorders has since been tested with prospective cohorts (maimaris_2014: few cohorts, inconsistent and attenuated associations) and co-twin designs (irons_2015), both in the library, and the authors themselves considered other associated factors the more likely explanation. The steep gradient is not in doubt as a description of what US adults reported in 1992; its causal reading remains open.

funding.funder: No funding or acknowledgment statement. Both authors were at the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (Division of Biometry and Epidemiology), which sponsored the NLAES (pp. 103–104).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Government researchers analysing their institute's own survey; no commercial interest is apparent.

what_would_settle_it: Designs that separate the effect of early drinking from shared liability: prospective cohorts that measure conduct problems, family environment and genetic risk before the first drink and record drinking and disorders as they happen; comparisons of twins or siblings who differ in age at first drink; and long-term follow-up of randomized prevention programmes that succeed in delaying first drinking.

domains.note: Adjusted for sex, race, age group, family history and duration of drinking; conduct problems, other psychopathology, childhood adversity, peer and family environment and other drug use were not measured; adjustment for current vs former drinking (and, in former drinkers, for duration up to the last drink) may itself be affected by the disorder.

One recalled question asked of adults of all ages; test-retest reliability 0.72; recall error, possibly differing between people with and without the disorder, cannot be ruled out; the authors acknowledge recall bias (p. 109).
Household survivors with good response (about 90%); deaths, institutions and homelessness, plausibly related to both early onset and severe disorder, are outside the frame.
Lifetime diagnoses; treatment after onset cannot remove a past diagnosis.
Numbers missing an onset age or a diagnosis, and cell sizes per onset age, are not reported.
Structured lay interview with fair to good reliability (0.73–0.76); lifetime episodes recalled in the same interview as the onset age; abuse counted only in people without dependence.
Only percentage reductions in odds are reported, without intervals, unadjusted estimates or model details; subgroup slopes compared without tests.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The steep crude gradient (Tables 1 and 2) is a sound description of what US drinkers reported in 1992, from a large probability sample with good response and a standard interview. As evidence that early drinking causes alcohol use disorders it is weak: the exposure was recalled in the same interview as the outcome, the main competing explanations (shared behavioural, psychiatric, family and genetic liability) were not measured, two covariates may follow from the outcome, and the adjusted estimates come without intervals. Cite it for the cross-sectional association and its size in 1992 (lifetime dependence above 40% for onset at 14 or younger against about 8% to 11% for onset at 20 or later, outside the bump at 23 and 24; 14% lower adjusted odds per year); do not cite it as showing that delaying the first drink prevents alcohol use disorders.

key_findings.finding: NLAES 1992: face-to-face Census Bureau interviews with 42,862 adults aged 18 and older in the noninstitutionalized population of the contiguous US, with oversampling of Black and young adult respondents; about 92% of selected households and 97.4% of selected respondents took part. The analysis used the 27,616 current (18,352) and former (9,264) drinkers: 13,990 men and 13,626 women; 3,062 Black and 24,554 nonblack respondents.
key_findings.locator: Method › Study Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 104); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 106); column heads of Tables 1 and 2 (p. 107)
key_findings.note: The text calls the drinkers 66% of the sample; 27,616 of 42,862 is 64.4% unweighted (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Age at onset was one recalled question (how old the respondent was on first starting to drink, not counting small tastes or sips), with test-retest reliability 0.72. Lifetime DSM-IV dependence and abuse came from the AUDADIS (reliability 0.76 for past-year and 0.73 for earlier diagnoses), abuse being counted only in people without lifetime dependence.

key_findings.note: The PDF's text layer misreads the onset-13 total as 41.3; the rendered page shows 47.3, which lies between the men's (49.4) and women's (43.2) values. Numbers of drinkers per onset age are not given.

key_findings.finding: Lifetime dependence was higher in men than women at every onset age, for example 41.3% vs 39.1% (12 or younger), 49.4% vs 43.2% (13), 19.4% vs 12.5% (18), 14.7% vs 7.4% (20) and 9.7% vs 6.9% (25 or older); in Black respondents it ranged from 44.4% (onset 13, SE 9.9) to 9.5% (onset 22).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Male, Female and Black columns
key_findings.note: The PDF's text layer misreads three values in Table 1 (men 25 or older 9.7 as 9.1; Black onset 15, 27.4 as 21.4; nonblack 25 or older 7.7 as 1.7) and one in Table 2 (Black onset 15, 9.7 as 9.1); the values here are from the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Weighted prevalence of lifetime alcohol abuse without dependence by age at first drink, all drinkers (SE): 12 or younger 8.3% (1.1); 13, 11.5% (1.8); 14, 13.8% (1.5); 15, 11.9% (0.9); 16, 10.6% (0.7); 17, 9.5% (0.6); 18, 7.8% (0.4); 19, 6.3% (0.6); 20, 4.8% (0.5); 21, 4.8% (0.4); 22, 4.9% (1.0); 23, 3.6% (0.9); 24, 3.1% (1.0); 25 or older, 2.5% (0.4). Editors' sums with Table 1 (the two diagnoses are mutually exclusive): any lifetime alcohol use disorder 48.9% (12 or younger), 58.8% (13), 54.6% (14), 24.4% (18), 16.2% (20) and 10.4% (25 or older).

After adjustment for sex, race, age group, duration of drinking, current vs former drinking and family history of alcoholism, with onset entered as a continuous term, the odds of lifetime alcohol dependence were 14% lower and the odds of lifetime abuse 8% lower for each later year of onset; no odds ratios, confidence intervals or p values are printed. Editors' conversion: odds ratios of about 0.86 and 0.92 per year.

By subgroup, the odds of dependence fell 14.7% (men), 13.2% (women), 14.5% (nonblack) and 8.1% (Black) per year of later onset, and the odds of abuse 7.0% (men), 9.1% (women), 6.7% (Black) and 7.8% (nonblack); no test of the differences between subgroups is reported.

The decline in dependence was interrupted by a rise from 9.5% (onset at 22) to 14.7% and 13.6% (onset at 23 and 24); the authors suggest, without data, that unusually late first drinking may mark other psychopathology and self-medication.

The authors identify ages 16 and younger as a particularly vulnerable period for starting to drink and say their results suggest prevention aimed at delaying onset until after 18 or 19, but that this recommendation should be considered cautiously because why onset relates to the disorders is not understood.

The authors call for a prospective study to find out whether the delay of drinking itself or, more likely, other associated factors explain the inverse relationship; whether early onset is a modifiable risk factor or a marker of disorders that would develop anyway; whether delaying onset has unintended effects such as more drug experimentation; and to reduce the recall bias of cross-sectional designs, including this one, and separate onset from duration of drinking.

reporting_issues.issue: The regression results are reported only as percentage reductions in odds: no coefficients, confidence intervals, p values, model sample size or unadjusted estimates, and no number of drinkers at each onset age.
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of the 14% and 8% figures, and how much adjustment changed them, cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results put the rise in dependence at onset ages 22 and 23 (p. 106), the Discussion at 23 and 24 (p. 108); Table 1 shows 9.5% at 22 and 14.7% and 13.6% at 23 and 24.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table settles it (23 and 24).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's pooled figures (abuse just over 11% for onset at 16 or younger and about 4% at 20 or older; dependence about 10% at 20 or older) do not appear in the tables, whose single-year values range from 8.3% to 13.8% (abuse, 16 or younger), 2.5% to 4.9% (abuse, 20 or older) and 7.9% to 14.7% (dependence, 20 or older).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the pooled values cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The drinkers are said to be 66% of the sample, but 27,616 of 42,862 is 64.4%; the sex and race shares given (51% and 49%; 88.9% and 11.1%), said to mirror the general population, equal the unweighted counts although Black respondents were oversampled (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; weighted and unweighted figures appear to be mixed without saying which is which.

reporting_issues.issue: The covariates include current vs former drinking and, for former drinkers, the duration of drinking up to the last drink (pp. 105–106), both of which can follow from developing a disorder; the effect of including them is not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjusted per-year estimates may be biased in either direction relative to the total association.
